title: Queen's Gambit Declined: model games
question: How do real games in the Queen's Gambit Declined turn a plan into a result, and at which moment could the other side still change course?
outcomes: Follows three real games (the Exchange Variation with a pawn storm, the Orthodox set-up with the e4 break, and a game where a loose bishop decided) and names for each the plan, the moment it became possible and the move that made it work
Counts the defenders of a bishop on h4 and sees what happens to it when the knight on f6 moves away (Bxe7 in game 1, the knight jump to g4 in game 3)
Checks the conditions of a pawn storm (the attacked king, the storming side's own king away, slow counterplay) and of the e4 break (finished development, rooks behind it)
Counts the attackers and guards of f7 before a sacrifice and finds the quiet follow-up that attacks two pieces
Separates what the engine says (depth 16) from what a player may have intended, and reads archive and master counts with their sample sizes

steps.text: **Three real games, one opening.** [S] The games below come from the Lichess broadcast database (CC0), which we keep locally: moves are facts, and each game is listed with its players, event and result. Your job is not to remember the moves. At each decision point, say what you would play and which plan it serves, then compare. The engine (depth 16) is evidence, not an explanation: it can say a move is better, not why a person would choose it.
steps.chapter: How to read a model game

steps.text: **What the numbers say first.** [V] Our masters data (both players 2500+, positions merged across move orders): after 3...Nf6, the exchange on d5 was played in 4,184 games (White scored 56%), the bishop to g5 in 813 (56%) and the knight to f3 in 739 (54%). [V] In our archive (broadcast games 2024 to 2026, both players 2500+), 254 reach 3...Nf6: White won 79, 136 were drawn and 39 were lost (58% for White). Our three games are three of those 254, so they show plans, not averages.

steps.text: **Why g4 can work.** [I] A pawn storm needs three things. Black's king must be on the attacked side. White's own king must not be in the way, so White has not castled. And Black's counterplay must be slower than the storm. In the Exchange the pawns usually have no targets; here White kept the king in the centre until the storm began. The engine rates 12.g4 level with its top choices (castling short or long) at depth 16: a sound plan, not the only one.

steps.prompt: In general: what should you check before a sacrifice that pulls the enemy king in front of its own queen? Write two conditions. [I] My list: the follow-up move must attack two things at once, and the recapture must not let the queen escape with a check.

steps.text: **What the three games share.** [I] In games 1 and 3 the knight left f6 and the bishop on e7 faced the bishop on h4. White took first in game 1 (Bxe7) and kept a small edge; in game 3 White took the knight, lost the bishop and had damaged pawns. In game 2 White traded on f6 early, so the question never arose. Both captures in game 3 leave Black slightly better; the loose bishop is what gave Black the choice.

steps.text: **What to remember.** A model game is a plan seen through its moments of choice. Find the moment, name the plan and its conditions, and ask what the other side could have done. Count the defenders of a loose bishop before you pin; count what a knight move uncovers before you allow it. [I] Three games are a few examples, not a rule: use them to ask better questions about your own games.

steps.prompt: Think of a recent game of your own with the Queen's Gambit Declined or another opening. Find one moment where a plan became possible. Write what the moment was and what the plan needed.
